claim: Carbon catabolite repression 4 (CCR4) is a conserved mRNA deadenylase regulating posttranscriptional gene expression.
source: Carbon catabolite repression 4 (CCR4) is a conserved mRNA deadenylase regulating posttranscriptional gene expression.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CCR4 function.

claim: The barley (Hordeum vulgare) CCR4 protein (HvCCR4) was identified to interact with the BYSMV phosphoprotein (P).
source: The barley (Hordeum vulgare) CCR4 protein (HvCCR4) was identified to interact with the BYSMV phosphoprotein (P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including GST pull-down, Co-IP, and BiFC assays.

claim: The BYSMV P protein recruited HvCCR4 from processing bodies (PBs) into viroplasm-like bodies.
source: The BYSMV P protein recruited HvCCR4 from processing bodies (PBs) into viroplasm-like bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization patterns.

claim: Overexpression of HvCCR4 promoted BYSMV replication in plants.
source: Overexpression of HvCCR4 promoted BYSMV replication in plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from minireplicon and full-length virus assays.

claim: Knockdown of the small brown planthopper CCR4 inhibited viral accumulation in the insect vector.
source: Conversely, knockdown of the small brown planthopper CCR4 inhibited viral accumulation in the insect vector.
evidence: This claim is supported by dsRNA knockdown experiments in planthoppers.

claim: HvCCR4 was recruited into N–RNA complexes by the BYSMV P protein.
source: Biochemistry experiments revealed that HvCCR4 was recruited into N–RNA complexes by the BYSMV P protein and triggered turnover of N-bound cellular mRNAs, thereby releasing RNA-free N protein to bind viral genomic RNA for optimal viral replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP and biochemical assays.

claim: HvCCR4 triggered turnover of N-bound cellular mRNAs.
source: Biochemistry experiments revealed that HvCCR4 was recruited into N–RNA complexes by the BYSMV P protein and triggered turnover of N-bound cellular mRNAs, thereby releasing RNA-free N protein to bind viral genomic RNA for optimal viral replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro deadenylation assays and RNA binding experiments.

claim: CCR4-mediated RNA decay releases RNA-free N protein to bind viral genomic RNA for optimal viral replication.
source: Biochemistry experiments revealed that HvCCR4 was recruited into N–RNA complexes by the BYSMV P protein and triggered turnover of N-bound cellular mRNAs, thereby releasing RNA-free N protein to bind viral genomic RNA for optimal viral replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased specificity of N binding to viral RNA in the presence of CCR4.

claim: Shortening of mRNA poly (A) tails, a process known as deadenylation, is the rate-limiting step in the mRNA decay process.
source: Shortening of mRNA poly (A) tails, a process known as deadenylation, is the rate-limiting step in the mRNA decay process (Garneau et al., 2007; Parker and Sheth, 2007; Houseley and Tollervey, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In eukaryotes, mRNA deadenylation is primarily mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex in RNA processing bodies (PBs).
source: In eukaryotes, mRNA deadenylation is primarily mediated by the CCR4-NOT complex in RNA processing bodies (PBs) that are dynamic cytoplasmic structures containing silenced mRNAs for degradation or translation repression (Parker and Sheth, 2007; Beckham and Parker, 2008; Xu and Chua, 2011; Miller and Reese, 2012; Chen and Shyu, 2013; McCormick and Khaperskyy, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CCR4-NOT complex is recruited to some specific mRNAs for deadenylation by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) such as Pumilio, Roquin, and Tristetraprolin.
source: Accumulating evidence shows that the CCR4-NOT complex is recruited to some specific mRNAs for deadenylation by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) such as Pumilio, Roquin, and Tristetraprolin (Leppek et al., 2013; Wahle and Winkler, 2013; Arae et al., 2019; Webster et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CCR4 and CAF1 are two deadenylases responsible for removing mRNA poly(A) tails in the CCR4-NOT complex.
source: In the CCR4-NOT complex, carbon catabolite repression 4 (CCR4) and CCR4 associated factor (CAF1) are two deadenylases responsible for removing mRNA poly(A) tails (Collart, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Plant CCR4 proteins do not contain LRR domains at their N termini.
source: While, plant CCR4 proteins do not contain LRR domains at their N termini (Dupressoir et al., 2001; Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and sequence analysis shown in figures.

claim: The N termini of plant CCR4 orthologues contain a zf-MYND-like domain that interacts with plant CAF1 proteins in the CCR4-NOT complex.
source: Instead, the N termini of plant CCR4 orthologues contain a zf-MYND-like domain that interacts with plant CAF1 proteins in the CCR4-NOT complex (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by BiFC data in the manuscript.

claim: Cellular mRNA decay is usually manipulated by viruses to complete viral life cycles due to limited functional proteins in viruses.
source: Cellular mRNA decay is usually manipulated by viruses to complete viral life cycles due to limited functional proteins in viruses (Ariumi et al., 2007; Beckham and Parker, 2008; Dougherty et al., 2011; McCormick and Khaperskyy, 2017; Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rhabdoviruses are negative-stranded RNA viruses that infect a wide range of organisms including plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates.
source: Rhabdoviruses are negative-stranded RNA viruses that infect a wide range of organisms including plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates (Ammar et al., 2009; Mann and Dietzgen, 2014; Dietzgen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rhabdoviruses share similar genome organizations encoding five structural proteins, including the nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and large polymerase (L) proteins in a conserved order 3′–N–P–M–G–L–5′.
source: Rhabdoviruses share similar genome organizations encoding five structural proteins, including the nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), and large polymerase (L) proteins in a conserved order 3′–N–P–M–G–L–5′.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rhabdovirus genome organization.

claim: The N protein entirely encapsidates the gRNA and antigenomic (ag) RNA to form N-RNA complexes that serves as templates for replication and transcription.
source: The N protein entirely encapsidates the gRNA and antigenomic (ag) RNA to form N-RNA complexes that serves as templates for replication and transcription (Ivanov et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The multiple functional P protein chaperones nascent RNA-free N (N0) by forming an N0–P complex that prevent N0 from binding nonspecifically to cellular RNAs.
source: The multiple functional P protein chaperones nascent RNA-free N (N0) by forming an N0–P complex that prevent N0 from binding nonspecifically to cellular RNAs, and attaches L protein polymerase complexes to the N-RNA complex (Ivanov et al., 2011; Leyrat et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P protein attaches L protein polymerase complexes to the N-RNA complex.
source: The multiple functional P protein chaperones nascent RNA-free N (N0) by forming an N0–P complex that prevent N0 from binding nonspecifically to cellular RNAs, and attaches L protein polymerase complexes to the N-RNA complex (Ivanov et al., 2011; Leyrat et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BYSMV was first reported in wheat fields of northern China in 2015.
source: In 2015, BYSMV was first reported in wheat fields of northern China (Di et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: BYSMV is obligately transmitted by the small brown planthopper (SBPH) in a persistent propagative manner.
source: BYSMV is obligately transmitted by the small brown planthopper (SBPH) in a persistent propagative manner (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The complete BYSMV genome encodes ten proteins in the order of 3′–N–P–P3–P4/P5–P6–M–G–P9–L–5′.
source: The complete BYSMV genome encodes ten proteins in the order of 3′–N–P–P3–P4/P5–P6–M–G–P9–L–5′ (Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A barley CCR4 fragment was identified amongst the IP products from GST-P immunoprecipitation from infected barley leaves.
source: The IP products were separated in SDS-PAGE gels and analyzed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and a barley CCR4 fragment was identified amongst the IP products (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Both plant and animal CCR4 proteins contain a conserved EEP domain in their C-termini.
source: Both plant and animal CCR4 proteins contain a conserved EEP domain in their C-termini (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in figures.

claim: Plant CCR4 orthologues harbor a zf-MYND-like domain at the N termini.
source: Plant CCR4 orthologues harbor a zf-MYND-like domain at the N termini (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in figures.

claim: The N terminus of LsCCR4 contains an LRR domain that is highly conserved in yeast and mammalian CCR4 orthologues.
source: while the N terminus of LsCCR4 contains an LRR domain that is highly conserved in yeast and mammalian CCR4 orthologues (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in figures.

claim: CCR4 protein accumulation increased in BYSMV-infected barley leaves at 15 dpi compared with mock plants.
source: Western blotting shows that CCR4 protein accumulation increased in BYSMV-infected barley leaves at 15 dpi (Figure 1B, left panel) and in BYSMV-minireplicon-infected N. benthamiana plants at five dpi (Figure 1B, right panels) compared with mock plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CCR4 protein accumulation increased in BYSMV-minireplicon-infected N. benthamiana plants at five dpi compared with mock plants.
source: Western blotting shows that CCR4 protein accumulation increased in BYSMV-infected barley leaves at 15 dpi (Figure 1B, left panel) and in BYSMV-minireplicon-infected N. benthamiana plants at five dpi (Figure 1B, right panels) compared with mock plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Accumulation of the CCR4 mRNA had no significant difference and even a little reduction in BYSMV-infected than in mock-treated plants.
source: However, qRT-PCR assays revealed that accumulation of the CCR4 mRNA had no significant difference (p<0.01) and even a little reduction in BYSMV-infected than in mock-treated plants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: BYSMV infections improve accumulation of host CCR4 protein rather than its mRNA.
source: These results demonstrate that BYSMV infections improve accumulation of host CCR4 protein rather than its mRNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blotting and qRT-PCR data showing increased protein but not mRNA levels.

claim: HvCCR4-His interacted with GST-P in vitro, but not with the GST control.
source: GST pull-down assays revealed that HvCCR4-His interacted with GST-P in vitro, but not with the GST control (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HvCCR4-Flag could efficiently immunoprecipitate P-GFP, but not GFP or P6-GFP.
source: At two dpi, Co-IP assays with agroinfiltrated N. benthamiana leaves show that HvCCR4-Flag could efficiently immunoprecipitate P-GFP, but not GFP or P6-GFP (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Co-expression of YC-P/YN-HvCCR4 and YN-P/YC-HvCCR4 resulted in production of YFP fluorescent punctate granules in the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast, co-expression of YC-P/YN-HvCCR4 and YN-P/YC-HvCCR4 resulted in production of YFP fluorescent punctate granules in the cytoplasm (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The fluorescent punctate granules of YN-P/YC-HvCCR4 moved rapidly throughout the cytoplasm.
source: Notably, these fluorescent punctate granules moved rapidly throughout the cytoplasm (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Video 1.

claim: Movement of the BiFC bodies of YN-P/YC-HvCCR4 was abolished when treated with the actin-depolymerizing agent 10 μM LatB.
source: Furthermore, when treated with the actin-depolymerizing agent 10 μM LatB, movement of the BiFC bodies of YN-P/YC-HvCCR4 was abolished in contrast to the highly dynamic movement in the DMSO control (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The BYSMV P protein and host HvCCR4 protein are components of mobile inclusion bodies that traffic along the actin/endoplasmic reticulum network.
source: These results, together with our previous results (Fang et al., 2019), reveal that the BYSMV P protein and host HvCCR4 protein are components of mobile inclusion bodies that traffic along the actin/endoplasmic reticulum network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the current manuscript and cited previous work.

claim: The BYSMV P protein contains three structural domains consisting of an N-terminal domain (PNTD, aa 9–33), a central domain (PCED, aa 60–183), and a C-terminal domain (PCTD, aa 208–270).
source: The BYSMV P protein contains three structural domains consisting of an N-terminal domain (PNTD, aa 9–33), a central domain (PCED, aa 60–183), and a C-terminal domain (PCTD, aa 208–270) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Coexpression of YC-P and YN-HvCCR4N resulted in production of BiFC fluorescent punctate granules, whereas YN-HvCCR4C did not associate with YC-P.
source: Coexpression of YC-P and YN-HvCCR4N resulted in production of BiFC fluorescent punctate granules, whereas YN-HvCCR4C did not associate with YC-P (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Both P60-183 and P208-295 associated with CCR4, but only P60-183 and CCR4 the association formed punctate granules similar to those of wild type BYSMV P.
source: Both P60-183 and P208-295 associated with CCR4, but only P60-183 and CCR4 the association formed punctate granules similar to those of wild type BYSMV P (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CCR4 did not affect self-interaction of BYSMV P in vitro and in vivo.
source: Moreover, we determined that CCR4 did not affect self-interaction of BYSMV P in vitro and in vivo using competitive GST pull-down and BiFC assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive GST pull-down and BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The N-terminal zf-MYND-like domain of HvCCR4 and the central BYSMV P domain (P60-183) are responsible for the P–HvCCR4 body formation.
source: Furthermore, the N-terminal zf-MYND-like domain of HvCCR4 and the central BYSMV P domain (P60-183) are responsible for the P–HvCCR4 body formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BiFC data showing which domains are required for punctate body formation.

claim: The P protein of northern cereal mosaic virus (NCMV) interacts with the N-terminal zf-MYND-like domain of HvCCR4.
source: Besides, we found that the P protein of northern cereal mosaic virus (NCMV), a close related cytorhabdovirus, interacts with the N-terminal zf-MYND-like domain of HvCCR4 using BiFC assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The P–CCR4 interaction is probably a common feature in cytorhabdoviruses.
source: These results demonstrate that the P–CCR4 interaction is probably a common feature in cytorhabdoviruses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both BYSMV and NCMV P proteins interact with CCR4.

claim: Arabidopsis and rice CCR4 are localized in processing bodies (PBs) that are foci for mRNA turnover in the cytoplasm.
source: Arabidopsis and rice CCR4 are localized in processing bodies (PBs) that are foci for mRNA turnover in the cytoplasm (Beckham and Parker, 2008; Chen and Shyu, 2013; Suzuki et al., 2015; Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HvCCR4-GFP and DCP1-mCherry co-localized in punctate cytoplasmic PBs.
source: As expected, HvCCR4-GFP and DCP1-mCherry co-localized in punctate cytoplasmic PBs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-P and HvCCR4-mCherry fluorescence were associated with trafficking punctate granules in cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, GFP-P and HvCCR4-mCherry fluorescence were associated with trafficking punctate granules in cytoplasm (Figure 2B and Video 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Video 4.

claim: The GFP-P granules were distinct from but adjacent to the DCP1-mCherry labeled marker PBs.
source: but the GFP-P granules were distinct from but adjacent to the DCP1-mCherry labeled marker PBs (Figure 2C, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The GFP-P bodies and DCP1-mCherry bodies trafficked and were adjacent with each other in cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, the GFP-P bodies and DCP1-mCherry bodies trafficked and were adjacent with each other in cytoplasm (Figure 2C, bottom panel and Video 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and Video 5.

claim: HvCCR4-GFP and CFP-P fully overlapped in punctate granules that were adjacent to DCP1-mCherry-labelled PBs.
source: To further investigate their co-localization, CFP-P, HvCCR4-GFP, and DCP1-mCherry were coexpressed in N. benthamiana leaves, and the results revealed that HvCCR4-GFP and CFP-P fully overlapped in punctate granules that were adjacent to DCP1-mCherry-labelled PBs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HvCCR4-GFP and DCP1-mCherry fully overlapped in P bodies when co-expressed with the BYSMV CFP-N protein.
source: In contrast, HvCCR4-GFP and DCP1-mCherry fully overlapped in P bodies when co-expressed with the BYSMV CFP-N protein (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fifty-eight among sixty HvCCR4-GFP bodies were adjacent to DCP1-mCherry bodies, while only two HvCCR4-GFP bodies were overlapped with DCP1-mCherry bodies in the presence of the CFP-P protein.
source: Quantitative analyses revealed that fifty-eight among sixty HvCCR4-GFP bodies were adjacent to DCP1-mCherry bodies, while only two HvCCR4-GFP bodies were overlapped with DCP1-mCherry bodies in the presence of the CFP-P protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most of HvCCR4-GFP bodies (fifty-six among sixty in total) were overlapped with DCP1-mCherry bodies in the presence of the CFP-N protein.
source: However, most of HvCCR4-GFP bodies (fifty-six among sixty in total) were overlapped with DCP1-mCherry bodies in the presence of the CFP-N protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The BYSMV P protein, rather than the N protein, hijacks host HvCCR4 from PBs in cytoplasm.
source: These results indicate that the BYSMV P protein, rather than the N protein, hijacks host HvCCR4 from PBs in cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the colocalization data showing different patterns with P versus N proteins.

claim: BYSMV P serves as a dynamic tethering protein to recruit the N and L proteins into viroplasm-like bodies that traffic along the ER/actin network.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that BYSMV P serves as a dynamic tethering protein to recruit the N and L proteins into viroplasm-like bodies that traffic along the ER/actin network (Fang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The YN-P/YC-L fluorescence colocalized with CFP-N and HvCCR4-mCherry.
source: As expected, the YN-P/YC-L fluorescence colocalized with CFP-N and HvCCR4-mCherry (Figure 3A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HvCCR4-GFP was recruited to the cytoplasmic granules together with CFP-N and L-mCherry in the presence of the BYSMV P protein.
source: Moreover, HvCCR4-GFP was recruited to the cytoplasmic granules together with CFP-N and L-mCherry in the presence of the BYSMV P protein (Figure 3B, upper panel)
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Without expression of BYSMV P, CFP-N and L-mCherry could not co-localized with the HvCCR4-GFP protein.
source: However, without expression of BYSMV P, CFP-N and L-mCherry could not co-localized with the HvCCR4-GFP protein (Figure 3B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HvCCR4-GFP, but not GFP, coprecipitated with N-Flag, L-Myc, and P.
source: Co-IP assays showed that HvCCR4-GFP, but not GFP, coprecipitated with N-Flag, L-Myc, and P (Figure 3C, compare lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of P protein expression, N-Flag did not coprecipitate with L-Myc or HvCCR4-GFP.
source: In the absence of P protein expression, N-Flag did not coprecipitate with L-Myc or HvCCR4-GFP (Figure 3C, compare lane 3), indicating that the P protein is a central tethering protein for the N, L and HvCCR4 protein complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Co-IP assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The P protein is a central tethering protein for the N, L and HvCCR4 protein complexes.
source: In the absence of P protein expression, N-Flag did not coprecipitate with L-Myc or HvCCR4-GFP (Figure 3C, compare lane 3), indicating that the P protein is a central tethering protein for the N, L and HvCCR4 protein complexes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Co-IP data showing P is required for complex formation.

claim: BYSMV P acting as a dynamic tethering protein efficiently recruit both viral proteins and host HvCCR4 into viroplasm-like bodies.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that BYSMV P acting as a dynamic tethering protein efficiently recruit both viral proteins and host HvCCR4 into viroplasm-like bodies, and suggest that the host HvCCR4 protein functions in virus replication and/or transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the colocalization and Co-IP data.

claim: The host HvCCR4 protein functions in virus replication and/or transcription.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that BYSMV P acting as a dynamic tethering protein efficiently recruit both viral proteins and host HvCCR4 into viroplasm-like bodies, and suggest that the host HvCCR4 protein functions in virus replication and/or transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the recruitment of CCR4 to replication bodies.

claim: Overexpression of HvCCR4 increased the numbers of RFP fluorescence foci at five dpi compared to the empty vector.
source: Compared to the empty vector (EV), overexpression of HvCCR4 increased the numbers of RFP fluorescence foci at five dpi (Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The HvCCR4N or HvCCR4C terminal derivatives did not increase the number of fluorescence foci.
source: but the HvCCR4N or HvCCR4C terminal derivatives did not increase the number of fluorescence foci (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The conserved Asn260 and Glu305 residues of HvCCR4 are essential for deadenylase activity.
source: The conserved Asn260 and Glu305 residues of HvCCR4 are essential for deadenylase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Chou et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overexpression of alanine-substituted mutant (N260A/E305A, designated CCR4mEEP) did not increase the fluorescence foci, compared with empty vector.
source: and overexpression of alanine-substituted mutant (N260A/E305A, designated CCR4mEEP) also did not increase the fluorescence foci, compared with empty vector (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HvCCR4 deadenylase activity substantially increases BYSMV agMR infections.
source: These results suggest that that HvCCR4 deadenylase activity substantially increases BYSMV agMR infections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the deadenylase-deficient mutant does not enhance infection.

claim: RFP accumulated to higher levels in HvCCR4 coinfiltrated tissues compared with those of EV, HvCCRN, HvCCRC, and HvCCR4mEEP.
source: Consistent with the numbers of fluorescence foci in infiltrated cells, RFP accumulated to higher levels in HvCCR4 coinfiltrated tissues compared with those of EV, HvCCRN, HvCCRC, and HvCCR4mEEP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of HvCCR4 had negligible effects on accumulation of BYSMV N and P.
source: In contrast, overexpression of HvCCR4 had negligible effects on accumulation of BYSMV N and P (Figure 4C), indicating improvement of HvCCR4 in MR infections was independent of N and P accumulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Improvement of HvCCR4 in MR infections was independent of N and P accumulation.
source: In contrast, overexpression of HvCCR4 had negligible effects on accumulation of BYSMV N and P (Figure 4C), indicating improvement of HvCCR4 in MR infections was independent of N and P accumulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blotting data showing no change in N and P levels.

claim: The full-length MR RNA abundance representative of MR replication increased to 2.28-fold in the HvCCR4 overexpression samples compared with the EV controls.
source: The full-length MR RNA abundance representative of MR replication increased to 2.28-fold in the HvCCR4 overexpression samples compared with the EV controls (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HvCCRN, HvCCRC, and HvCCR4mEEP co-expression had negligible effects on MR replication.
source: In contrast, HvCCRN, HvCCRC, and HvCCR4mEEP co-expression had negligible effects on MR replication (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All the samples had similar transcription activities.
source: In addition, we evaluated transcription activities by normalizing the RFP mRNA levels relative to the gMR template, showing that all the samples had similar transcription activities (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: HvCCR4 promotes minigenome replication, but not virus transcription.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that HvCCR4 promotes minigenome replication, but not virus transcription.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing increased replication but not transcription.

claim: HvCAF1 contains a classical PXLXP motif that interacts directly with the CCR4 N terminus.
source: We first cloned the full-length cDNA sequence of barley CAF1 and analyzed the amino acid sequence of HvCAF1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and found that HvCAF1 contains a classical PXLXP motif that interacts directly with the CCR4 N terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HvCAF1 interacts with the HvCCR4 N terminus, but has compromised affinity with the HvCCR4 C terminus.
source: As expected, BiFC analysis shows that HvCAF1 interacts with the HvCCR4 N terminus, but has compromised affinity with the HvCCR4 C terminus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BYSMV P does not interact with HvCAF1 in BiFC assays.
source: In addition, our results show that BYSMV P does not interact with HvCAF1 in BiFC assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both BYSMV P and HvCAF1 interact with the Mynd-like domain of HvCCR4.
source: It should be noted that both BYSMV P and HvCAF1 interact with the Mynd-like domain of HvCCR4.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the BiFC data showing both proteins interact with the N-terminal domain.

claim: Overexpression of HvCAF1 resulted in substantially decreased cell numbers of fluorescence foci at five dpi.
source: In contrast, overexpression of HvCAF1 resulted in substantially decreased cell numbers of fluorescence foci at five dpi (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RFP accumulated to a much lower level in HvCAF1 overexpressed leaves, but accumulated to a higher level in HvCCR4 overexpressed leaves compared with empty vector infiltration.
source: Western blotting analysis consistently showed that RFP accumulated to a much lower level in HvCAF1 overexpressed leaves, but accumulated to a higher level in HvCCR4 overexpressed leaves compared with empty vector infiltration (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HvCAF1 negatively affects BYSMV minigenome infections, in contrast to HvCCR4 enhancement.
